The Gospels are the first four books of the New Testament—Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John—which form the primary historical and theological records of Jesus's life, ministry, death, and resurrection. Written in the decades following Jesus's crucifixion, they blend eyewitness testimony, theological interpretation, and narrative artistry to present Jesus as Messiah and Son of God. The Gospels are the foundation of Christian faith and have been the most intensely studied and debated texts in Western literature. Their four distinct portraits of Jesus offer complementary yet sometimes divergent perspectives. Matthew presents the Jewish Messiah, Mark the suffering servant, Luke emphasizes Jesus as the friend of the marginalized, and John portrays him as the divine Word. Together, they form a lens through which billions of Christians have understood their faith.

Gospel derives from Old English godspell, translating Greek euangelion, meaning "good news"—the announcement of salvation through Jesus. Written primarily in Greek in the late first century CE, decades after Jesus's death, they blend oral tradition, eyewitness memory, theological reflection, and literary artistry. All four were considered canonical and authoritative by the second century CE, though numerous other gospels circulated in early Christian communities.

Matthew, Mark, and Luke are called the Synoptic Gospels because they share remarkably similar structure, sequence, and sometimes identical wording. Mark is the earliest, composed around seventy CE. Matthew and Luke independently used Mark plus a hypothesized sayings collection. Matthew emphasizes Jesus as the Jewish Messiah fulfilling Old Testament prophecy. Luke emphasizes compassion for the poor, women, and Gentiles. Both expand on Mark's narrative.

John is theologically distinct. It opens with a philosophical prologue declaring Jesus the Word made flesh and presenting him as divine from the outset. Where the Synoptics feature parables, John features long theological discourses such as "I am the bread of life" and "I am the way, the truth, and the life." John structures Jesus's ministry around seven miracles and three Passover visits to Jerusalem, emphasizing symbolism and mystical meaning over chronological narrative.

Traditionally, Matthew and John are attributed to apostles, while Mark is attributed to Peter's companion and Luke to Paul's companion, though scholars debate these attributions. In medieval Christian art, the four Gospels are symbolized by winged creatures: Matthew as a winged man, Mark as a winged lion, Luke as a winged ox, and John as an eagle.
